claims.claim: Gladstone says an elision in a Wolfe text can carry large implications a casual reader will not see.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: vast churning implications invisible to the casual reader

claims.claim: Gladstone describes reading Wolfe as assembling clues by touch in the dark rather than being told.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: We fumble through darkness, trying to assemble clues by touch.

claims.claim: Gladstone says some details Wolfe plants are the author's signature to the audience rather than evidence about the story world.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: Wolfe loves to include winking asides between author and audience.

claims.claim: Floyd Holland characterises Wolfe's prose as dense and built with parentheticals and complicating clauses.
claims.source: Floyd Holland, 'The Enchanting Prose of Gene Wolfe' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: the dense prose, interjecting itself with parentheticals and complicating clauses

claims.claim: Holland says Wolfe never lets a sentence run away from him, reading an aura of control across the prose.
claims.source: Floyd Holland, 'The Enchanting Prose of Gene Wolfe' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: One never feels he let a sentence get away from him

claims.claim: Holland attributes the beauty of Wolfe's otherwise unwieldy sentences to word choice and confidence of construction.
claims.source: Floyd Holland, 'The Enchanting Prose of Gene Wolfe' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: made beautiful by careful word choice and a certain confidence of construction

claims.claim: Wolfe, quoted by Holland, said real people are unreliable narrators all the time.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, quoted by Floyd Holland (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: Real people really are unreliable narrators all the time

claims.claim: Holland says the opening scene of The Fifth Head of Cerberus carries clues to a larger mystery while reading as ordinary recollection.
claims.source: Floyd Holland, 'The Enchanting Prose of Gene Wolfe' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: the scene is peppered with clues to the larger story

claims.claim: In a sentence-level reading of the opening paragraph of The Fifth Head of Cerberus, Alex notes it shows no genre markers at all.
claims.source: Alex, 'Whose Afraid of the Big Bad Wolfe?' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: There are no obvious genre trappings in this opening paragraph, at all.
claims.page: section 'What can an opening teach you?'

claims.claim: Alex says what is absent from Wolfe's opening paragraph, not what is present, is what is notable about it.
claims.source: Alex, 'Whose Afraid of the Big Bad Wolfe?' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: What’s noticeable here is not what’s present but what’s missing.
claims.page: section 'What can an opening teach you?'

claims.claim: Alex says the opening grounds the reader in concrete spatial description of the narrator's house, naming the orientation of its wings and courtyard.
claims.source: Alex, 'Whose Afraid of the Big Bad Wolfe?' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: grounded in a narrator’s spatial description that is concrete
claims.page: section 'What can an opening teach you?'

claims.claim: Alex says Wolfe makes odd details register as stranger by setting them among mundane ones.
claims.source: Alex, 'Whose Afraid of the Big Bad Wolfe?' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: weird details feel all the weirder when they are grounded

claims.claim: Alex says the detail Wolfe leaves unexplained reads as more real than an explanation of it would.
claims.source: Alex, 'Whose Afraid of the Big Bad Wolfe?' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: These little opacities feel ‘realer’ than any explanation of them would.

claims.claim: Alex says the brothers' unexplained soundless gestures imply a private life the reader is never given access to.
claims.source: Alex, 'Whose Afraid of the Big Bad Wolfe?' (Substack), 2025
claims.quote: hint at a private life that the reader never gets access to

claims.claim: Writer Matthew Sini says Wolfe's sentences work at the level of rhythm and structure.
claims.source: Matthew Sini, 'Great Uncle Gene', New Mythologies (Substack), 2023
claims.quote: they hit at the level of rhythm and structure
